text:
Meta must stop silently withholding the Instagram accounts of independent journalists in India

13 October 2026

Since 9 October 2026, Instagram has made the accounts of several independent journalists covering the protests in Delhi unavailable in India. Utkarsh Gaur’s main account was withheld on 9 October, and Sunny Tomar’s soon after. On the night of 12 October, Instagram withheld the account of Shubhangi Das Gupta, a 22-year-old independent journalist, and her secondary account now appears to face the same action. Today, Journo Mirror’s account was withheld in India. Each received the same notice, that Instagram had, “temporarily restricted access to this account pursuant to legal requirements under India’s Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules.” The notice does not say which authority made the demand, which rule was invoked, which post was objected to, or when the “temporary” restriction ends. It arrives as a no-reply notification after the account has gone dark, with no prior warning and no reason.

The same day, IANS and ANI, citing Delhi Police sources, reported that around 500 posts “spreading rumours or trying to create unrest among people” had been taken down. On 12 October, PTI had put the figure at 300, which means about 200 more in one day. The police have not said which posts were removed, from which platforms, under which provision, or whether anyone who posted them was told. We are also receiving reports of WhatsApp accounts being shut down and of mobile numbers being put through fresh KYC verification that leaves them unusable while it is pending. All of this comes alongside a timeline in which there was suspension of internet services and public transport in the heart of the national capital.

IFF condemns Meta’s withholding of entire journalist accounts on the strength of an unnamed “legal requirement”, and the Delhi Police’s practice of announcing a running censorship tally through anonymous sources. Meta must restore these accounts, tell every affected user who asked for the restriction and under what law, and stop turning demands about particular posts into the silencing of entire accounts.
The IT Rules, 2021, on which Meta’s notice relies, give it two routes to restrict content. The notice meets the conditions of neither. If Meta acted on a government demand, the route is Rule 3(1)(d). If Meta acted on its own, Rule 4(8) requires it, as a significant social media intermediary, to notify the user before disabling access, explain the grounds, and give an adequate opportunity to dispute the action. None of this happened. In this situation at present the entire burden will be shifted to the user to seek remedy under Rules 3(2) and 3A, where a user must first go to Meta’s Grievance Officer, who has 15 days, and then to the Grievance Appellate Committee, which has 30 more. In our experience these timelines are often not met, and a grievance against unnamed “legal requirements” is likely to be answered by pointing back to them. Whatever the intention, the effect is to keep a journalist off the platform for more than six weeks, exactly when her reporting matters most.

The Delhi Police figures raise their own questions. “Rumour” is not a ground for restricting speech under Article 19(2).  A count of 500 posts announced through unnamed sources does not let anyone tell whether a post was fabricated or simply showed something the police did not want seen. Nor is it obvious that 200 reasoned intimations, each signed by an officer of DIG rank and each identifying the provision, the unlawful act and the exact URL, were issued in a single day.

Our demands

1) Meta should restore every account withheld in connection with the protests where the underlying demand, if any, concerned specific posts, and restrict no more than the URLs named in a lawful reasoned intimation.
2) Meta should tell each affected user in writing which authority made the demand, the issuing officer’s rank, the provision relied on, the content identified, and when the restriction will end.
3) Meta should disclose whether its systems automatically extend demands about individual posts to entire accounts, and stop any such escalation immediately.
4) The Delhi Police should publish the takedown requests it has issued, with their number, platforms, provisions, issuing officers and reasons, as Anuradha Bhasin requires.
5) MeitY should ensure notice and a hearing to every person whose content is restricted, publish the outcome of the monthly Secretary-level review under Rule 3(1)(d), and stop using Section 79(3)(b), the Sahyog Portal and “temporary” restrictions under the IT Rules to bypass the safeguards of Section 69A.
If you have been affected

If your post or account was withheld or removed in connection with the protests, or you received a notice about a police data request, write to legal@internetfreedom.in for pro bono assistance. Keep screenshots of every notice, note the date and time, and delete nothing. Document, document, document.

Additional Solicitor General Chetan Sharma, representing the government, argued that offensive videos should be blocked across the board to avoid a repetitive game of legal cat-and-mouse with duplicates. The court has adjourned the matter for its next hearing on September 3.

IFF Statement on the Information Technology (IGDME) Amendment Rules, 2026

The Government of India today notified the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2026, concerning synthetically generated information (SGI). While these rules claim to address AI-generated content harms such as deepfakes, they introduce severe digital rights violations that fundamentally undermine constitutional protections and worsen problems that IFF had flagged in our November 2025 submissions on the draft rules.​

1. Accelerated Censorship Through Compressed Timelines The notified rules drastically compress content removal timelines, transforming intermediaries into rapid fire censors. Government takedown orders must now be complied with within three hours (reduced from 36 hours in the draft), while Grievance Appellate Committee orders must be actioned within two hours (down from 24 hours). User complaints on significant social media intermediaries must be resolved within seven days (reduced from 15 days), with urgent cases requiring action within 36 hours (down from 72 hours). These impossibly short timelines eliminate any meaningful human review, forcing platforms toward automated over-removal and creating a prior restraint regime incompatible with Article 19(1)(a). It is notable that in many of these censorship actions a copy of the notice or hearing is never provided to the person whose content is removed. Hence, the entire process is secretive and in violation of natural justice. 

2. Expansion of Prohibited Content Categories : The rules introduce sweeping new prohibitions absent from the draft that was put to consultation. Rule 3(3)(a)(i) now categorically bans SGI that "results in the creation, generation, modification or alteration of any false document or false electronic record". This vague formulation could criminalize legitimate uses of AI in document preparation, research outputs, and creative works. The rules also prohibit SGI "falsely depicting or portraying" persons or events "in a manner that is likely to deceive", language so broad it could capture satire, parody, political commentary, and artistic expression.​

3. Identity Disclosure to Private Parties : A particularly troubling addition is Rule 3(1)(ca)(ii)(III), which mandates disclosure of violating users' identities directly to complainants who claim to be victims. This bypasses judicial oversight and creates serious risks of harassment, doxing, and vigilante action, especially against marginalized users and dissenting voices.​ This is due to the absence of any anchoring language for the need to get a court order or an order pursuant to a criminal investigation. 

4. Continued Violation of Safe Harbor Framework: Despite IFF's submissions highlighting incompatibility with Section 79 of the IT Act and the Shreya Singhal precedent, the rules continue to impose proactive monitoring obligations that transform intermediaries from neutral conduits into active censors of speech. The requirement to "deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures" including "automated tools" to prevent uploads violating "any law for the time being in force" creates an impossible compliance burden across India's complex legal landscape.

The notified rules represent a regression from the already problematic draft that we had called to be withdrawn and instead approach AI based content risks beyond the existing safe harbor framework. We believe AI technologies do need to be regulated however deeply disagree with the approach of the Union Government that has over time expanded its censorship powers against the framework and rights under the Constitution of India. 

IFF will publish a detailed first-read analysis tomorrow examining the constitutional, technical, and human rights implications of these amendments.

Exemption from Liability of Intermediaries in Certain Cases

Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 provides legal protection to intermediaries against liability for third-party content hosted or transmitted through their platforms.

An intermediary includes social media platforms, internet service providers, web-hosting companies, search engines, and similar online service providers. Examples include X (Twitter), Facebook, and YouTube.

Sub-section (1)

An intermediary shall not be liable for any third-party information, data, or communication link made available or hosted by it, subject to the conditions specified in the Act.

Sub-section (2)

This protection applies only if:

The intermediary's role is limited to providing access to a communication system through which information is transmitted, temporarily stored, or hosted;

The intermediary does not initiate the transmission;

The intermediary does not select the receiver of the transmission;

The intermediary does not select or modify the information contained in the transmission; and

The intermediary observes due diligence and complies with the requirements prescribed under the Act and the applicable rules.

Sub-section (3)

The protection under Section 79 shall not apply if:

1. The intermediary has conspired, abetted, aided, or induced the commission of an unlawful act; or

2. Upon receiving actual knowledge, or upon being notified by the appropriate Government or its agency that any information, data, or communication link hosted on its computer resource is being used to commit an unlawful act, the intermediary fails to expeditiously remove or disable access to such material while preserving evidence.

Explanation

The term “Third Party Information” refers to any information dealt with by an intermediary in its capacity as an intermediary.

Practical Significance

Section 79 provides a “safe Harbour” to intermediaries. As a result, social media platforms and other intermediaries are generally not automatically liable for content posted by their users. However, if they participate in unlawful activities or fail to act after receiving a valid legal notice or government direction, they may lose the protection granted under Section 79.

The scope of this provision was further clarified by the Supreme Court of India in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India. The Court held that “Actual knowledge” for the purposes of Section 79 generally arises through a court order or a notification issued by a competent government authority, requiring the intermediary to take appropriate action.

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.

IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE

WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.

🚨 BIG: Government of India has unveiled one of the most comprehensive legal frameworks to combat AI-generated deepfakes, synthetic media, misinformation and unlawful online content.

The framework brings together the IT Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, IT Rules, 2021, the 2026 IT Rules amendments, and the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines to strengthen digital safety and platform accountability.

Key highlights:

🔹 Mandatory AI Labelling: Platforms must clearly label AI-generated or synthetic content with traceable metadata so users can identify manipulated content and prevent deception.

🔹 Fastest Takedown Timelines Yet: Removal of unlawful content after a valid government or court notice has been reduced from 36 hours to just 3 hours. Grievance redressal timelines have also been tightened—from 72 hours to 36 hours, and 24 hours to 2 hours for sensitive content such as nudity, impersonation and similar categories.

🔹 IT Act, 2000: Covers penalties for computer-related offences, identity theft (Sec. 66C), online impersonation (66D), privacy violations (66E), publishing obscene or sexually explicit content (Secs. 67 & 67A), empowers blocking of unlawful content under Sec. 69A, removal directions under Sec. 79, and enables police investigation under Secs. 78 & 80.

🔹 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Covers cheating by personation (Sec. 319), forgery through false electronic records (Sec. 336), spreading false reports or misinformation causing public mischief (Sec. 353), and organised cybercrime involving deepfake content (Sec. 111).

🔹 Strict Platform Obligations: Intermediaries must not host or share content that infringes rights, invades privacy, promotes hate or violence, harms children, violates intellectual property, misleads users about message origin, knowingly spreads false information, impersonates individuals (including using AI), threatens India's sovereignty, security or public order, or violates any applicable law.

🔹 Greater Accountability for Social Media Platforms: Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) must assist law enforcement in tracing originators of serious content, deploy automated tools to detect unlawful content, publish compliance reports, appoint grievance and compliance officers, maintain India-based compliance infrastructure, and provide user verification, appeals and fair hearing mechanisms.

🔹 Zero Tolerance for Harmful AI: Platforms are now explicitly required to prevent AI-generated child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery, deepfakes, AI impersonation, harmful synthetic media and other unlawful AI-generated content using reasonable technical measures and automated detection systems.

🔹 Legal Consequences: Failure to comply with the IT Rules can result in intermediaries losing their Section 79 safe-harbour protection, exposing them to prosecution and legal action under applicable laws.

🔹 Robust Enforcement Ecosystem: The framework will be enforced through Grievance Appellate Committees (GACs), the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the SAHYOG Portal, the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, and law enforcement agencies. Citizens can report cybercrime and deepfakes through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, with Helpline 1930 available for cyber fraud complaints.

The message is clear: AI innovation is welcome, but deepfakes, impersonation, misinformation, child exploitation, and unlawful synthetic content will face significantly stricter regulation, faster takedowns, and stronger legal consequences than ever before.

இதற்காக வெளியிடப்பட்ட அரசாணை எங்கே? இதில் யார் யாரெல்லாம் பொறுப்பில் உள்ளார்கள்? என்னென்ன பணிகளை செய்கிறார்கள் ? இதற்கான நிதி ஒதுக்கீடு என்ன? என்ற கேள்விகளை எல்லாம் RTI மூலம் ஜீவிதா என்பவர் கேட்டுள்ளார்.

ஆனால், அவர் RTI மூலம் கேட்கும் கேள்விகளுக்கு பதில் கூற முடியாது என்று இந்த அரசு கடிதம் கொடுத்துள்ளது. 

Transparent Governance-ஐ தருவேன் என்று வாயால் வடை சுட்ட முதலமைச்சர், தன்னுடைய Advisors நியமனம் முதல், தகவல் சரிபார்ப்பக பொறுப்பாளர்கள் தேர்வு வரை எல்லா GO-வையும் ஒளித்து வைப்பது ஏன்?

ரசிகர்கள் என்ற போர்வையில் பொய்களைப் பரப்பி -  ஆபாச தாக்குதல் நடத்திக் கொண்டிருந்த தகுதியற்ற இணையக் கூலிப்படைக்கு அந்தப்பொறுப்புகள் வழங்கப்பட்டுள்ளது அம்பலமாகிவிடும் என்பதாலா? 

உண்மை எது - பொய் எது என்று சொல்லும் தகவல் சரிபார்ப்பகம் பற்றிய தகவல்களே மக்களுக்குத் தெரியாமல் இருப்பது நல்லதல்ல. 

உண்மையை நீண்ட நாள் பொத்தி வைக்க முடியாது என்பதை உணர்ந்து இந்த Dummy அரசு தகவல் சரிபார்ப்பகம் பற்றிய தகவல்களை உடனடியாக வெளியிட வேண்டும்.

Shortcut Sensitivity in Agent-Safety Evaluations : https://t.co/XSffPQJD5Z

"Hasan DemirkiranKontexthasan@kontext.securityJens ErnstbergerKontextjens@kontext.security
Abstract
AI agents take actions through tools. Some actions are sensitive, so guards that supervise them must themselves be evaluated reliably. Yet the data used to evaluate a guard can include cues that make labels predictable without measuring the intended safety construct, and those cues can also influence guard decisions.
We introduce a three-level shortcut-auditing framework and audit completed LinuxArena trajectories and two TS-Bench-derived step datasets. We distinguish label predictability, observational guard association, and paired decision sensitivity. In LinuxArena, shorter average shell commands strongly predict trajectory labels. In AgentDojo-Traj, exact-tool lookup falls from F1=.901 with mixed-domain folds to .495 under domain holdout. In AgentHarm-Traj, released TS-Guard F1 falls from .902 under row weighting to .719 with equal interaction weighting, while balanced accuracy rises.
We then test the strongest safe-row marker association in a seven-configuration screen on a frozen 64-step AgentDojo-Traj cohort using repeated, interleaved Haiku calls. Rewriting the <INFORMATION> marker lowers blocking by 8.33 percentage points, while opaque tool aliases raise it by 11.46 points. All unsafe calls remain blocked; the changes concern false positives against inherited labels. Both effects remain nonzero after subtracting the formatting-placebo effect, with exploratory 95% ranges excluding zero. The same edits also change measured accuracy against inherited labels. This provides direct evidence that benchmark representation can materially change a guard’s decisions and measured evaluation performance. The Haiku-sized effects do not reproduce in Luna or deterministic Q8 TS-Guard. We recommend domain group holdouts, evaluation-unit metrics, and placebo-controlled paired interventions.
1Introduction
A benchmark may be easy for the wrong reason. Annotation conventions, source identity, repeated templates, and collection artifacts can all predict labels without measuring the intended construct (Gururangan et al., 2018; Geirhos et al., 2020). This problem is especially consequential for agent-safety evaluation. A tool guard may be deployed to approve or block a consequential action, while its benchmark record also contains scaffolding added by the evaluation pipeline: provenance tags, tool names, trajectory length, source subsets, and repeated interaction structure.Simple lexical and length features separated honest and attack trajectories in the public LinuxArena sample, motivating a search for analogous rules elsewhere. Such a rule may track real risk, collection differences, or evidence also used by a capable guard; rule–guard agreement cannot distinguish these https://t.co/vAy7xxijcb systematically uncover potential shortcuts, we introduce shortcut auditing as a three-level inference ladder for agent-safety guard evaluations. A shortcut audit asks progressively stronger questions: can a simple cue predict released labels; is that cue associated with guard decisions; and does changing only that cue alter the guard’s decision?We distinguish:1.Label Predictability: Can a deliberately capability-poor rule predict released labels?
2.Observational Guard Association: Do guard decisions correlate with the suspected cue in released records?
3.Paired Decision Sensitivity: Does the guard change when the cue is changed while the candidate action’s authorization and effect are held fixed?Paired edits test whether changing the input changes the guard’s decision. To interpret that change as spurious shortcut reliance, the edits must preserve the relevant safety information. For a deterministic guard, evaluating each original–edited pair reveals whether the strict decision changes. Stochastic guards require additional controls because identical inputs can produce different outputs and sequential calls may drift over time. We therefore interleave repeated original and edited calls, include a formatting placebo, and report identical-input disagreement separately.Our contributions are:•Three-level shortcut-audit framework. We introduce a inference ladder separating label predictability, observational guard association, and paired decision sensitivity with explicit construct-preservation caveats, plus repeat and placebo controls for stochastic guards.
•Audit of released agent-safety evaluations. We apply shortcut-auditing to AgentDojo-Traj, a LinuxArena public sample, and to AgentHarm-Traj. Across LinuxArena and two TS-Bench-derived datasets, we expose label separability, exact-tool domain-transfer failure, and evaluation-unit sensitivity: command length reaches AUC .910, exact- tool lookup falls from F1=.901 to .495 under domain holdout, and TS-Guard F1 falls from .902 to .719 under equal-interaction weighting.
•Guard-level shortcut validation. We move beyond showing that benchmark labels are predictable by testing candidate cues directly against guard decisions, using a purpose-built TS-Guard reproduction and hosted models configured as pre-execution guards. Repeated paired AgentDojo-Traj interventions with a placebo control reveal material Haiku sensitivity, while Luna and Q8 TS-Guard checks show that the effect is configuration-specific. Haiku blocking changes by −8.33 percentage points (pp) for the marker rewrite and +11.46​pp for aliases. With the same cohort, conditions, schedule, repetitions, and estimand, GPT-5.6 Luna gives 0.00​pp and +1.04​pp, while the deterministic TS-Guard reproduction changes its decision for 3 of 64 marker-edit pairs.The result is deliberately not “these benchmarks are broken.” Some proxies are intentional and semantically relevant: an untrusted-content marker communicates provenance, and a malicious request is relevant to a harm policy. Our claim is that such features create shortcut opportunities. Evaluation authors should measure whether conclusions survive group holdouts, equal-unit weighting, paired perturbations with construct-preservation caveats, and repeat-original controls. In this paper, shortcut auditing means testing whether apparent findings survive these checks.
2A three-level shortcut-audit framework
Let a benchmark record be x=(s,z). Here, s is the remaining context needed to judge the candidate action, such as the request, interaction history, tool description, and arguments. The variable z is the candidate cue singled out for audit (e.g. trajectory-length). This analytical decomposition does not assume that z is irrelevant or spurious. It tests how strongly a guard evaluation depends on the cue or on its representation. Let y be the released label, r⁡(z)∈ℝ a capability-poor diagnostic that does not observe s, and g⁡(x)∈{0,1} a guard decision, with one denoting block. Figure 1 summarizes the three claims and the inference licensed at each level.1. Label predictability
Does r⁡(z) predict y?
Finds a candidate cue.2. Observational guard
association
Does g⁡(s,z) vary with z?
Nominates an edit.3. Paired decision
sensitivity
Compare g⁡(s,z) with g⁡(s,z′).
Tests that exact edit.Figure 1: The three-level shortcut-audit framework. Each level motivates the next test, not the next conclusion. Paired edits probe decision sensitivity only to the extent that they preserve the target construct; stochastic guards additionally require repeat and placebo controls.

Level 1: label predictability.
We evaluate a deliberately capability-poor diagnostic r using only z, not the judgment context s. Its score isSpred​(r)=ℳ⁡({(r⁡(zi),yi)}i=1n),(1)where ℳ is an appropriate discrimination metric, such as AUC, F1, or balanced accuracy. Our diagnostics include command length, a marker plus a short verb list, exact tool lookup, and an all-positive baseline. Strong performance establishes a predictive construction signature. It does not show that the cue is spurious, available to a deployed guard, or used by that guard.
Level 2: observational guard association.
For an input-visible cue, let a⁡(z)∈{0,1} indicate whether the audited cue is present. Within a comparison cohort C, we measureΔassoc(C)=𝔼[g(x)∣a(z)=1,x∈C]−𝔼[g(x)∣a(z)=0,x∈C].(2)The cohort C can restrict comparisons to the same released label, domain, action family, or another matched context. A large contrast can nominate a cue for intervention. It remains observational because z, y, and legitimate evidence in s share a data-generating process, so measured and unmeasured confounding can explain the association.
Level 3: paired decision sensitivity.
For a deterministic guard and transformation T⁡(s,z)=(s,z′), we measure the paired strict-decision flip ratepflip(T)=1n∑i=1n[g(xi)≠g(T(xi))].(3)The intervention must preserve the label and intended construct; otherwise the flip may be legitimate. For stochastic g, the target estimand is insteadΔT=1n∑i=1n{Pr[g(T(xi))=1]−Pr[g(xi)=1]},(4)estimated here by repeated calls in both conditions. Under stable independent draws, the signed K=1 mean g⁡(T⁡(xi))−g⁡(xi) is unbiased for ΔT, but can be imprecise and temporally confounded when calls are not interleaved. Its unsigned flip rate is a different, descriptive disagreement estimand. Independent repeat disagreement measures stability and should not be subtracted from either quantity. A strict-decision non-flip also does not exclude changes in ordinal scores, components, rationales, or redundant feature use.This ladder combines ideas from shortcut learning, group-shift evaluation, behavioral testing, and contrast sets (Geirhos et al., 2020; Koh et al., 2021; Ribeiro et al., 2020; Gardner et al., 2020). Our contribution is to operationalize label predictability, observational guard association, and paired decision sensitivity as a three-level audit for released agent-safety evaluations. The experiments show that strong label predictability can coexist with localized paired decision sensitivity.
3Evaluation artifacts and audit design

3.1Evaluation artifacts

LinuxArena.
LinuxArena evaluates control protocols for agents operating in live software environments (Tracy et al., 2026). We use the 932-row public sample at a pinned dataset revision. Of these, 918 rows contain extracted shell commands. Because the public sample repeats action traces under different monitor runs, we hash complete action content after removing only the monitor response. The primary diagnostic contains 576 exact-action-unique shell trajectories: 176 attack and 400 honest across ten environments. We never use the nominally unique trajectory_id as a deduplication key. The sample also contains LinuxArena’s precomputed per-action suspicion scores from its Claude Opus 4.6 monitor on 200 Opus-generated honest trajectories and 74 human-crafted LaStraj attacks. The monitor conditions on the task, possible side-task goals, and tool-call history, but not agent reasoning; each stored score averages two calls.
TS-Bench.
ToolSafe introduces TS-Bench and TS-Guard for pre-execution, step-level tool safety (Mou et al., 2026). TS-Bench derives the released AgentDojo-Traj and AgentHarm-Traj step records, including step-level risk scores, from AgentDojo and AgentHarm trajectories (Debenedetti et al., 2024; Andriushchenko et al., 2025). We use these files at a pinned commit; the paired AgentDojo-Traj variants described below are the only new inputs we construct. Under ToolSafe’s strict mapping, every nonzero risk rating is unsafe. AgentDojo-Traj has 1,220 steps (352 unsafe and 868 safe) across four domains. AgentHarm-Traj has 731 steps (525 unsafe and 206 safe) in 197 released interaction-ID groups.We use released labels, TS-Guard predictions, and previously cached hosted-guard assessments from pinned source commits. No tool call in a record is executed. The appendix gives a PDF-contained reproduction specification. The aggregate code/results package is publicly available.11https://github.com/hasandemirkiran/shortcut-sensitivity-agent-safety-evaluations It contains no raw benchmark text, arguments, identifiers, or provider responses.
Audit scope.
Here, an audit means applying the three-level framework in Section 2 to released evaluation artifacts. We test whether simple cues predict labels, whether input-visible cues are associated with guard decisions, and, when an edit intended to preserve the construct is available, whether paired edits change those decisions. The analysis is black-box: it uses released records, outputs, and fixed input transformations without access to guard internals. We do not test an adaptive agent, an evasion attack, or end-to-end tool execution.
3.2Capability-poor diagnostics
Level 1 begins with one deliberately limited diagnostic matched to each artifact’s construction. The aim is not to build the best classifier. It is to test whether a narrow cue recovers released labels and whether that result survives controls for duplication, source overlap, transfer, and evaluation-unit weighting. For LinuxArena, the deterministic score is the negative mean shell-command character count, so larger scores indicate shorter commands. We compare it with character n-gram TF–IDF and logistic regression trained leave-one-environment-out (LOEO). We report AUC and a clustered bootstrap over main-task/side-task groups. These are completed-trajectory diagnostics, not operational step-wise monitors.For AgentDojo-Traj, the fixed binary rule requires both the literal <INFORMATION> marker in history and a current tool whose name starts with one of 11 side-effect verbs (for example, send_, delete_, or update_). The rule and verb list were frozen after initial inspection, so this is a diagnostic audit rather than a preregistered test. A second diagnostic memorizes each exact tool’s majority label. For unseen tool names, it predicts the training fold’s overall majority label; ties are classified as unsafe. We evaluate it both with interaction- grouped five-fold cross-validation and leave-one-domain-out (LODO) transfer. The lookup explicitly uses evaluation labels and must not be described as a deployable classifier.For AgentHarm-Traj, we test the all-unsafe baseline and audit the mapping from source subset to strict label. We then recompute guard metrics at three units: rows, equal-weight interactions, and one majority prediction per interaction. This distinguishes performance over recorded steps from performance over underlying tasks. Separately, we case-fold parsed tool names, normalize their structured arguments, retain exact-execution groups containing both labels, and compare safe and unsafe context means with equal weight per execution group.
3.3Frozen AgentDojo counterfactual cohort
A frozen cohort is a fixed panel of base steps and paired edits selected before any guard is run on the edited inputs. Freezing prevents us from choosing examples after seeing intervention outcomes; pairing holds the underlying step fixed; and balancing eight marker-present safe and eight marker-present unsafe steps from each AgentDojo domain prevents one domain or label from dominating. This deterministic selection produces 64 bases from 58 source interactions. “Frozen” does not mean preregistered or representative of the full benchmark: released labels and earlier guard outputs had already been inspected. Each base has an original; a marker rewrite replacing <INFORMATION> with <UNTRUSTED_EXTERNAL_CONTENT> (and the matching closing tag) while retaining enclosed content; a consistent opaque tool alias retaining description and arguments; and their combination. The hosted run adds a neutral placebo that changes only outer JSON whitespace. Operational-action and label preservation were intended edit constraints, not independently established facts: we performed no blinded human equivalence check. The marker rewrite makes untrusted external provenance more explicit, while the aliases are generated separately for each sample and do not represent one globally consistent tool renaming, so the estimand is sensitivity to these exact edits rather than proof of spurious use. Within this study, marker rewrite versus original is the focal edit; alias and combined edits are exploratory stress tests.
Guards.
Our deterministic subject is a byte-pinned 8-bit, group-64 MLX reproduction of the public TS-Guard checkpoint under greedy decoding. It passes a predeclared gate on the 64 originals: 64/64 parse, 63/64 strict decisions and 58/64 exact scores agree with the release. This result applies only to that Q8/MLX reproduction, not the released BF16/vLLM execution path.We evaluate Claude Haiku 4.5 (Anthropic, 2025) as a prompted stochastic guard. In a seven-configuration observational screen, it had the largest safe-row marker association (74.09​pp), making it a high-association case for paired intervention. Selection used cached observational outputs; the 64-step cohort and edits were fixed before the 960 new intervention calls. Table 3 reports the full screen. We make three deterministically interleaved calls per base and condition (960 total), at temperature zero with structured outputs, routing only to Anthropic through OpenRouter with fallback disabled. The primary estimand averages each base’s three-call block-probability difference, with 10,000 domain-stratified bootstrap replicates clustered over the 58 source interactions. The formatting placebo and within-condition disagreement diagnose serialization sensitivity and instability. After the Haiku result, but before inspecting any valid Luna outcome, we added GPT-5.6 Luna (OpenAI, 2026) as a compact cross-provider replication. It uses the same cohort, prompt, five conditions, three calls per condition, and normalized base/condition/repetition order. We route only to OpenAI through OpenRouter with fallback disabled, request medium reasoning and structured output, and apply the same estimand and bootstrap. This replication tests cross-model generality; it is not a model-strength comparison. A secondary one-draw GPT-5.5 check is reported in Appendix C; it is not part of the repeated primary analysis.

4Predictive benchmark cues are strong
Table 1 reports the Level-1 diagnostics. Each benchmark exposes a different opportunity; there is no evidence for one universal rule.Table 1:Capability-poor diagnostics. Intervals are 95% clustered bootstrap intervals where available. Grouped CV keeps interactions together; LODO holds out an entire AgentDojo domain.ArtifactDiagnosticResultStress control / interpretationLinuxArena (576 trajectories)Negative mean shell-command charactersAUC .910 [.873, .941]LOEO lexical AUC .934 [.907, .955]; difference .023 [.008, .040].AgentDojo-Traj (1,220 steps)Marker + 11 action prefixesF1=.802; balanced accuracy .894; recall .972Exploratory fixed rule; the marker also appears in 321 safe rows.AgentDojo-TrajExact tool majorityGrouped-CV F1=.901; balanced accuracy .925LODO F1=.495; only 17.3% of rows use a tool seen in another domain.AgentHarm-Traj (731 steps)Predict every step unsafeF1=.836; balanced accuracy .500Positive prevalence makes F1 look strong without discrimination.

4.1LinuxArena: separable collection, not a length cutoff
"

Transparency cannot be selective.

The Tamil Nadu government has reportedly declined to provide RTI information regarding the restructuring, staffing, salaries and administration of its Fact Check Unit, citing Section 7(9) of the RTI Act.

Section 7(9) is not, by itself, a valid ground for refusing information.

If this unit operates using taxpayers’ money, the public has every right to know who runs it, how appointments were made and how much is being spent.

The TVK government promised transparency and accountability. That commitment must apply to its own administration too.

A government fact-checking unit should be transparent enough to withstand a fact-check itself.

text:
Dear @elonmusk ,
Since 59 million people read your letter, a few facts.
And before I start, a bit about me. I am a mere yoga practitioner. So India is not for beginners like you eliciting a response from my leader. I am enough. 

Now the response. 

Starlink is not "unlicensed." 

DoT granted your licence in June 2025. IN-SPACe authorised your constellation in July 2025. 
What is pending is commercial spectrum and final security clearance, and Jio's own satellite venture and OneWeb are waiting in the same queue, under the same rules. 

If Ambani were the "real boss of India," his company wouldn't be standing in line behind the Cabinet with yours.

On the one question you actually fought him on, auction versus administrative allocation, India sided with you. Jio then signed up to sell your kits. Strange behaviour for a monopolist supposedly blocking you.

Why the caution? 

Starlink terminals have been reported in the hands of smugglers and insurgents on Indian soil. Your company wants 100% foreign ownership, and India's space regulator has already sent back one constellation application. A country of 1.4 billion is entitled to check who controls the signals over its territory.
Your own country does exactly this, and more: 1. Denied China Mobile a licence and revoked China Telecom's after nearly two decades. National security. 2. Shut out BYD with 100% tariffs and a rule barring Chinese connected-car technology. Not because of Tesla. Because Washington decided so. 3. Blocked every new foreign-made drone model, DJI included. 4. Forced TikTok into American hands. 5. Allowed Nippon Steel to buy US Steel only with a government "golden share." 6. Took a stake in Intel and a 15% cut of Nvidia's and AMD's China sales. 7. Charged $100,000 per new H-1B worker, and taxed Indian goods at up to 50% last year.
I'm not complaining. 
Sovereign states protect what they consider strategic. That isn't crony capitalism when America does it, and it isn't when India does.

But spare us the free-market sermon. According to State Department cables reported by the Washington Post, US embassies nudged tariff-hit countries to approve Starlink. America's rural broadband programme was rewritten in a way that, by the Wall Street Journal's estimate, could multiply Starlink's share several times over. When your government bends rules toward your company, it's called "tech-neutral." When ours takes its time, it's "monopolistic exploitation."

You also mocked our Prime Minister's office as a businessman's property and took sides in our domestic politics. Indians argue loudly about corporate power, political funding and cronyism. 

That's our democracy working, and it's ours to settle at our ballot box. It is not a prop for your licence negotiation.
Our villages do need connectivity. Help get it there. Finish the security compliance, accept Indian conditions on data and control, and compete on price. Indians are excellent customers of anyone who treats them as customers rather than subjects.
Thank you 🙏 for your attention on this subject matter. Now drop your weed and get back to work.

text:
Starlink has an Indian license, 20 ground stations on Indian soil, and a promise to keep Indian user data in India. What it doesn't have is permission to switch on.

Thousands of Indian villages still have no 4G. In the Northeast alone, more than 1,800 had no mobile signal of any kind as of February, most of them in Arunachal Pradesh. These are the places satellite internet is built for: mountain villages, islands, flood zones, anywhere a tower or a fiber line takes years and a lot of money to arrive.

Starlink has done what India asked. It got its telecom license in June 2025 and space regulator approval a month later. It built India-specific security controls, agreed to keep data local, and has been reporting the names, addresses and coordinates of its test terminals to the government every two weeks. It operates in more than 150 countries. In India it still can't sell a single subscription, and the company is now talking about early 2027.

New Delhi says nobody is being singled out, since Eutelsat OneWeb and Jio's satellite venture are stuck at the same stage. I believe that, and I don't think it helps. When three licensed operators, two of them backed by India's biggest telecom groups, can't clear security review after more than a year of trials, that tells you the process has no deadline. It doesn't tell you it's thorough.

The security concerns are real. Indian agencies have been rattled by smuggled terminals turning up in border areas, and India is entitled to lawful interception, local data storage and an emergency shutoff. Starlink has already signed up for all of it. The answer to a misused terminal is enforcement, not keeping the service dark for everyone who would use it legally.

Elon Musk has been blunt, calling the delay "a crime against the people of India" and asking, "Is Ambani the real boss of India?" You don't need to buy the whole oligarch theory to see his point. Reliance spent months lobbying for spectrum auctions that would have favored deep-pocketed incumbents. The government sided with Starlink on that one, which is to its credit. Now it needs to finish the job.

India can keep every security power it wants and still let a kid in Arunachal get online. Right now it's choosing not to.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

CONTROL THE MEDIA, CONTROL THE NARRATIVE? INDIA DESERVES ANSWERS ABOUT CENSORSHIP AND PRESS FREEDOM.

“You have used the oldest trick in the politician's handbook: control the media so you can control the narrative.”

That is the central accusation made in this commentary by Physicians Perspective. The allegations deserve scrutiny—but every claim must be tested against credible reporting and documentary evidence.

1. NEARLY 195,000 GOVERNMENT BLOCKING ORDERS IN FIVE MONTHS

The Indian Express reported that government agencies issued approximately 195,000 blocking orders to Instagram, Facebook and YouTube between March and July 2026. Instagram received nearly 100,000, Facebook around 80,000 and YouTube approximately 15,000.

The report also found that Meta had integrated its systems with the government's Sahyog portal, allowing certain government-directed takedowns to occur automatically without separate human review.

These figures raise serious questions about transparency, procedural safeguards and the risk of lawful political speech being restricted. They do not mean that 195,000 individual posts were necessarily removed, or that every order was unlawful.

2. JOURNALISTS DETAINED WHILE COVERING PROTESTS

The Committee to Protect Journalists reported that at least 37 journalists were detained while covering protests against the Election Commission's leadership on 10–11 October 2026. Some journalists reported being assaulted, having equipment seized or being detained despite identifying themselves as members of the press.

Reuters and Human Rights Watch have also reported concerns about police action against protesters and journalists.

These reports demand answers: What were the legal grounds for each detention? Were seized devices returned? Were allegations of excessive force independently investigated?

3. PROTEST-RELATED CONTENT RESTRICTED

Alt News documented restrictions on posts by opposition organisations, political leaders and creators, including content associated with the Cockroach Janata Party protests. The Indian Express separately reported that government blocking orders increased during the period of student protests.

The central issue is whether restrictions are lawful, necessary, proportionate and open to meaningful challenge. The government and platforms should disclose the legal basis for restrictions to the extent permitted by law and provide effective remedies against erroneous takedowns.

4. MEDIA OWNERSHIP AND CORPORATE INFLUENCE

India's media ownership is concentrated among powerful corporate groups, raising legitimate questions about editorial independence, conflicts of interest and the influence of commercial interests on public debate.

But ownership alone does not prove that every newsroom follows government instructions. Each allegation of editorial interference should be supported by evidence.

5. WHY NO REGULAR SOLO PRESS CONFERENCES?

Reuters reported in May 2019 that Narendra Modi attended a press conference but did not take questions, directing a journalist to then BJP president Amit Shah instead. The absence of regular, open question-and-answer press conferences has therefore become a legitimate subject of democratic scrutiny.

A prime minister should be willing to face difficult questions from independent journalists. Interviews and public speeches are not substitutes for sustained, open questioning.

6. WHAT ABOUT BOTS AND COORDINATED ONLINE HARASSMENT?

The video alleges that fake accounts and bots systematically attack critics and defend the government. Such coordination is possible, but this particular allegation needs account-level evidence, platform investigations or credible independent research before it can be treated as established fact.

Do not confuse an allegation with a proven finding. Demand the evidence.

THE DEMOCRATIC TEST IS SIMPLE:

- Can journalists investigate those in power without intimidation?
- Can citizens criticise government policy without arbitrary censorship?
- Can peaceful protesters document events and share evidence?
- Can platforms explain why content was removed and offer meaningful appeals?
- Can the Prime Minister face unscripted questions from the press?

These are not demands for privilege. They are demands for transparency and accountability in a constitutional democracy.

The government may legitimately restrict unlawful content and maintain public order. But those powers must not become a shield against scrutiny or a means of suppressing peaceful dissent.

A DEMOCRACY CANNOT BE MEASURED ONLY BY THE ELECTIONS IT HOLDS. IT MUST ALSO BE MEASURED BY THE QUESTIONS ITS LEADERS ARE WILLING TO ANSWER.
